title: Your first program from scratch
goal: Assemble the main.c structure. Write lines with quotation marks inside the text and predict the exact result.

prerequisites.text: You know how to build and run main.c. You can tell output apart from a compiler diagnostic.

terms.title: Header
terms.definition: A file containing declarations. stdio.h declares standard input and output functions.

terms.title: Statement
terms.definition: An action in the code. A puts call in this lesson ends with a semicolon.

terms.title: Escape sequence
terms.definition: A notation starting with a backslash. Inside a string, \" represents one quotation mark in the text.

sections.title: The structure and its contents
paragraphs: A short program starts by including the declarations it needs. Next is int main(void): int relates to the exit status and void here means main takes no parameters. A pair of braces marks its body.
Calls inside the body go in order. The argument of puts is a string literal. Its outer quotes are needed in the source and do not appear in the output.
When a quotation mark belongs in the message, write \" inside the string. The backslash tells the compiler that the next quote is part of the text.

sections.title: A queue display with quotation marks
paragraphs: Type the program into a new main.c. Predict the two lines of output, ignoring the delimiters of each literal.
steps: Including stdio.h makes the declaration of puts available.
The first call prints Queue, a space and A in quotation marks. The compiler translates each \" into one printed quotation mark.
The second puts starts the next line after the first. return 0 reports successful completion.
trace: The quotes around A are part of the text
Only the two lines appear in stdout

sections.title: When a quote ends the text too early
paragraphs: If you type puts("Queue "A"");, the first inner quote prematurely ends the string. The compiler can no longer read the call as one argument. Put a backslash before each inner quote.
If you want quotation marks solely as source delimiters, escapes would add unwanted characters to the output. Check which quotes are part of the requested text.

sections.title: Print a new card of your own
paragraphs: A new printer issues a three-line check-in card. It differs from the queue display in purpose, lettering, number and number of lines. Break the request into three independent calls.
If everything fits on one line, check how many puts calls you have and their arguments. Compare output character by character before opening the solution.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Specifies the form of main, string literals and the puts call.

selfcheck.prompt: What is the first output line?
feedback: Correct. The inner marks print and the outer marks delimit the literal.
The outer quotation marks do not print.
The backslashes encode the quotation marks in the source.

selfcheck.prompt: Why does puts("Queue "A""); not express a single text argument?
options: The unescaped inner quote terminates the literal
The semicolon belongs inside the argument
feedback: Correct. Escape the quotation marks that belong to the message.
puts prints string literals that contain letters.
The ; ends the entire statement after the call.

selfcheck.prompt: What do the outer and escaped inner quotation marks each do?
selfcheck.feedback: Distinguish the syntax that delimits a literal from quotation marks that are part of the data. In this example the backslashes are used only in source notation.

practice.title: A check-in card
practice.task: Print exactly three lines: CHECK IN, Desk "B", Ticket 8. Use three puts calls and the standard main.c structure. The second line contains printed quotation marks.
criteria: The lines are in the required order with no empty line.
Exactly two quotation marks surround B.
You can explain the role of stdio.h and return 0.
practice.hint: The second literal needs two \" escapes. Its outer quotes remain ordinary delimiters.

steps.expected: The second line contains Desk and a quoted B.

steps.action: Replace Card and add two calls.
steps.why: This keeps the three actions distinguishable.
steps.expected: The program builds and prints three lines.

steps.action: Check spaces, quotes and ticket number.
steps.why: Line count alone does not check content.
steps.expected: The result matches character by character.

exercises.title: Transfer the idea
exercises.task: Make a copy for a different desk. Print Desk "C" and Ticket 11 while leaving the first line alone. Explain why the number of lines stays the same.
criteria: You change the arguments to two calls while preserving the number of commands.

teaching.scene: At a hall entrance, a sign displays a queue name in quotes and the next ticket number. Build both lines and check which quotation marks the visitor actually sees.

predict.prompt: The first puts source line contains backslashes next to A. Which characters are visible around A, and which message appears on the second line?
predict.answer: Inside the literal, each \" sequence encodes one quote. The visible lines are Queue "A" and Next: ticket 3. The outer quotation marks delimit the source text.

apply.prompt: A kiosk needs the output Line "C". Where would you put backslashes to get exactly two printed quotes?
apply.answer: Put a backslash before each of the two interior quotes. Look for the single visible line Line "C".

practice.strategy: Set up the header and main first. Add the three calls one at a time and build after adding the line with quotes.
practice.diagnosis: A build error near B can point to a literal closed too early. Inspect both literal delimiters and the escape before each printed quote.

syntax.explanation: The opening and closing `"` delimit the literal. The `\"` sequences inside those delimiters encode the two visible double-quote characters.
syntax.mistake: Outer quotes surround the argument. Printed double quotes inside that argument require `\"`.
